entries.question: Who was Timnah?
entries.summary: Genesis 36:12 identifies Timna as a woman, specifically the concubine of Eliphaz son of Esau, who bore Amalek to him. 1 Chronicles 1:36 lists 'Timna' as one of the sons of Eliphaz alongside Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, and Amalek. Same name, same father, different gender and different relationship. The sister-of-Lotan verses in Genesis 36:22 and 1 Chronicles 1:39 are not a separate contradiction; they are additional genealogical detail about the same woman.
entries.commentary: The sharp contradiction here is Genesis 36:12 against 1 Chronicles 1:36, and it is a straightforward gender-and-relationship problem. In Genesis 36:12 Timna is a woman who is the concubine of Eliphaz and who bears him a son named Amalek. In 1 Chronicles 1:36 the Chronicler's list of Eliphaz's sons reads 'Teman, Omar, Zephi and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna and Amalek' — Timna appearing as one of Eliphaz's sons. A woman does not belong on the sons list, and a concubine is not a son. That is the actual tension. The Lotan's-sister verses (Gen 36:22 and 1 Chr 1:39) get sometimes swept into the contradiction as a third claim about Timna's identity, but they don't contradict Genesis 36:12 at all. A woman can be both Lotan's sister in her Horite family of origin and later the concubine of Eliphaz in her marital household. Those are just two biographical data points about the same person viewed from two genealogical angles. Folding them into the contradiction weakens the case, because it conflates a real textual problem with a non-problem. Keep the spotlight on Genesis 36:12 versus 1 Chronicles 1:36. Apologists handle the real contradiction a few ways. Archer and Keil-Delitzsch argue that 1 Chronicles 1:36 is elliptical: 'and Timna and Amalek' is short for 'and by Timna, Amalek,' drawing on Genesis 36:12's detail that Timna bore Amalek. This is a reasonable attempt, and it would harmonize the two lists if granted. The problem is that it requires inserting words that aren't in the Masoretic Text and treating a woman's name on a sons list as a prepositional phrase about her maternity. Sara Japhet in the Old Testament Library commentary notes that the Chronicler frequently condenses and occasionally garbles earlier genealogical material, and Gary Knoppers in the Anchor Bible 1 Chronicles 1-9 points out that the Septuagint preserves variant readings in exactly this passage, reinforcing that the list shows signs of transmission trouble. The more parsimonious reading is that the Chronicler was working from a version of the Edomite genealogy that listed Timna differently, or that the text has been corrupted somewhere in its transmission. Either way, the contradiction between Genesis 36:12 and 1 Chronicles 1:36 as they now sit in the MT is real. The Lotan's-sister data isn't.

entries.question: Does God have a body?
entries.summary: Genesis shows Yahweh strolling through Eden 'in the cool of the day' — audible footsteps, physical movement. John 4:24 and Luke 24:39 then insist God is a spirit who by definition has no flesh and bones. Take your pick: a wandering-through-the-garden deity, or an incorporeal one.
entries.commentary: The apologist move is to call Genesis 3:8 anthropomorphism — God stooping to human language the way a parent uses baby-talk. Gleason Archer runs this play in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and Walton in his NIVAC Genesis commentary treats the 'walking' as a theophanic accommodation to human limits. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. But the critical read is more parsimonious: early Israelite Yahwism straightforwardly pictured a corporeal deity, and the later philosophical spirit-God of Hellenistic Judaism and the Johannine community is a theological upgrade, not an original feature. Mark Smith's The Early History of God and Benjamin Sommer's The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel document a robust 'divine body' tradition across the Hebrew Bible — Yahweh eats with Abraham at Mamre, wrestles Jacob, reveals his back to Moses. Sommer's own focus is the Hebrew Bible's divine-body tradition rather than Johannine reception, but his work fits within a broader scholarly picture in which 'God is spirit' looks more like a later philosophical development than an original Israelite axiom. The contradiction is real; the harmonization is an attempt to read later metaphysics back into the earliest strata of the text.

entries.question: Does God know and see everything?
entries.summary: 1 John 3:20 declares God knows all things. Genesis 3 shows Yahweh wandering the garden asking 'Where art thou?' — an omniscient being doesn't search for the humans he supposedly sees always and everywhere. The contradiction is between a philosophical claim of universal knowledge and a narrative God who has to ask questions.
entries.commentary: Apologists routinely read Genesis 3:9 as a rhetorical or pedagogical question — God isn't actually ignorant of Adam's location; he's giving Adam the chance to confess. Archer runs this line, and Hamilton's NICOT Genesis makes a similar move. Fair enough as a pastoral reading, but the text itself shows no such signal. Walton's Lost World of Genesis One pushes a cognitive-environment approach where Genesis portrays God in anthropomorphic terms because that is how ancient Near Eastern audiences encountered deities. That concession is the honest one — and it's the critical position: the Yahwist (J) source pictures a limited deity who walks, asks, changes his mind, and reacts to events. The systematic theology of omniscience is a much later development, crystallized through Hellenistic Jewish writers like Philo and later Christian scholastics. James Kugel in How to Read the Bible calls this the 'small God' of early Israel — a deity with real cognitive limits whose personality the redactors never fully scrubbed out. The apologist harmonization requires importing centuries of philosophical theology into a text that doesn't supply it.

entries.question: Is everyone descended from Adam and Eve?
entries.summary: Genesis 3:20 names Eve the mother of all living, and Paul treats universal Adamic descent as the engine of original sin. Hebrews 7:3 then describes Melchizedek as having no father, no mother, and no genealogy — which breaks the universal-descent claim in exactly one verse.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist read, running from Calvin through modern evangelical commentators like William L. Lane in the Word Biblical Commentary on Hebrews, is that Hebrews 7:3 is a literary/typological observation: Melchizedek's genealogy is simply not recorded in Genesis 14, and the author of Hebrews is leveraging that silence to build a Christological type for Jesus' priesthood. That is the strongest version of the harmonization and it has real force — the author of Hebrews is doing Philonic-style allegorical exegesis, not biology. But the contradiction bites at the level of what the text literally asserts. Harold Attridge's Hermeneia Hebrews commentary notes the author pushes the argument beyond mere silence into ontological claims — Melchizedek is 'made like unto the Son of God.' Craig Koester's Anchor Bible Hebrews reaches the same conclusion: the author is reading Genesis 14 through a second-Temple lens where Melchizedek had become a heavenly or semi-divine figure (see 11QMelchizedek at Qumran). So the Bible is internally tangled: Genesis assumes universal Adamic descent, Hebrews inherits a Second Temple Melchizedek tradition where he isn't descended from anyone, and the two don't reconcile without deciding which text gets to speak literally. The critical verdict is that 'everyone descends from Adam' is a Priestly theological claim, and Hebrews is drawing on a completely different mythological stream.

entries.question: Does God respect anyone?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Deuteronomy, 2 Chronicles, Acts, Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, 1 Peter
entries.summary: Genesis 4 has Yahweh preferring Abel's offering and rejecting Cain's — he respects persons. A seven-verse stack from Deuteronomy, 2 Chronicles, Acts, Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, and 1 Peter then insists God is no respecter of persons. The Hebrew Bible shows explicit favoritism; the New Testament stack, and a few Old Testament echoes, deny it exists.
entries.commentary: The apologist move here rests on a lexical distinction: the Hebrew and Greek phrases translated 'respect of persons' (Hebrew nasa panim, Greek prosopolempsia) mean partiality in judgment — accepting bribes, favoring the rich over the poor in court. God preferring Abel isn't that; it's divine assessment of the heart. Blomberg, Archer, and more recently Thomas Schreiner in his Romans commentary all run this line. That distinction is real and worth granting — the Greek term in Romans 2:11 is a technical loanword from legal contexts. But the distinction only partially solves the problem. Yahweh's preference for Abel in Genesis 4:3-5 has no stated reason in the text itself; readers supplied 'heart' reasons later (Hebrews 11:4 claims it was by faith). The Yahwist narrator just says Yahweh preferred the meat offering to the vegetable one — which critics from Westermann onward read as an etiological myth legitimating animal sacrifice and the herder lifestyle over agriculture. Walter Moberly's chapter on Cain and Abel in The Theology of the Book of Genesis, and David Carr in Reading the Fractures of Genesis, both note that the narrative does not give a stated reason for Yahweh's preference — which is exactly what a respect-of-persons act looks like from the outside. So the harmonization works for Romans 2 in a courtroom sense but strains when Genesis 4 is left in its narrative nakedness.

entries.question: Does God desire animal sacrifices?
entries.summary: The Priestly source and the Genesis narrative have Yahweh approving Abel's animal sacrifice and later filling Leviticus with hundreds of verses of mandatory blood offerings. Psalms 40, 50, and 51 then say God does not desire sacrifice or burnt offerings at all. The cult system the Torah makes compulsory is what the Psalter, and later the prophets, dismiss as unwanted.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization is that the Psalms and prophets are not rejecting sacrifice as such — they're rejecting sacrifice without contrition. Derek Kidner's Tyndale commentary on Psalms and Tremper Longman both argue for a 'relative negation' reading: what God really wants is obedience and a broken heart, not mechanical ritual. That is a standard rabbinic and Christian reading and it has textual support — Psalm 51 does pair the rejection with a call for a contrite heart. But the critical read pushes harder. Jacob Milgrom's monumental Anchor Bible Leviticus volumes and Jonathan Klawans in Purity, Sacrifice, and the Temple argue that these passages reflect a real internal dispute in ancient Israel between temple-cult insiders and prophetic/sapiential critics — an actual historical conflict between the P/H priestly tradition and a non-cultic piety stream visible in certain Psalms and in prophets like Amos and Hosea. Put bluntly: the Bible preserves competing schools on whether Yahweh wanted the slaughter at all. The harmonization flattens what is actually a polyphonic argument inside the text. Take your pick — but you cannot read all of these verses as one coherent voice.

entries.question: What became of Cain?
entries.summary: Genesis 4:11-12 has Yahweh cursing Cain to be a fugitive and a vagabond on the earth — no settled life, no rest. Four verses later Cain settles in the land of Nod, marries, fathers Enoch, and founds a city. The curse and the subsequent narrative directly contradict.
entries.commentary: Kenneth Mathews in his NAC Genesis volume and Bruce Waltke in his Genesis commentary both try to harmonize this by saying 'fugitive and vagabond' describes Cain's psychological or moral state rather than his physical condition — he's a spiritual wanderer even while building a city. That is the apologist playbook, page one: redefine the concrete language of the curse into an abstract metaphor. The critical read is cleaner. Source critics from Wellhausen to Richard Friedman have long noted that Genesis 4 stitches together two distinct Cain traditions: a curse-and-wandering narrative (the Kenite tradition that explains a nomadic people's protective mark) and a city-founding genealogy that functions as an etiology for urban civilization. Westermann's Genesis 1-11 commentary treats the city-founding as a separate source fragment incorporated into the Yahwistic narrative. The contradiction is a seam, not a coherent portrait — it shows the Torah's editors preserving competing traditions about the same figure rather than forcing one clean story. Mathews' harmonization papers over the seam with pastoral theology. The plainer reading is that the J source had more than one Cain tradition on file.

entries.question: Is polygamy OK?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, 1 Timothy, Titus
entries.summary: This one is a three-way tangle. The Hebrew Bible narrates polygamy without condemnation across patriarchs, judges, and kings — Abraham, Jacob, Gideon, David, Solomon, Rehoboam all pile up wives. Genesis 2:24 frames marriage as one man and one woman becoming one flesh. The Pastoral Epistles then restrict monogamy specifically to bishops, implying laypeople can still have multiple wives.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization runs through dispensationalism and ideal-versus-permitted categories: Genesis 2 states the creation ideal, the patriarchal and monarchic polygamy is narrative description under divine tolerance (not endorsement), and the Pastorals tighten things for church leaders. Blomberg and Köstenberger both run versions of this. That scaffolding is doing enormous work to reconcile a corpus that never once condemns polygamy outright. The critical read is more direct. Deuteronomy 21:15-17 regulates polygamy rather than prohibits it. David Instone-Brewer in Marriage and Divorce in the Bible and the Ancient Near East documents that Second Temple Jewish sources show polygamy remained legal and practiced among Jews into the first century. The Pastoral Epistles' 'husband of one wife' (mias gunaikos andra) phrase is disputed — it may mean 'faithful to one wife,' 'married only once' (prohibiting remarriage after divorce or widowhood), or literally 'monogamous.' Luke Timothy Johnson's Anchor Bible commentary on the Pastorals walks through all three readings without endorsing one. Meanwhile Genesis 2:24 describes the creation-week pairing, not a universal marriage law. So the Bible's actual position on polygamy is: tolerated, never commanded, never explicitly banned, and later ecclesiastical limits applied only to leadership. Modern Christian monogamy is a post-biblical norm read back into the text.

entries.question: Was Enoch the sixth or the seventh from Adam?
entries.summary: Count Adam as position one and the Genesis 5 genealogy puts Enoch at position seven. Count Adam as position zero and he's the sixth. Jude 14 says 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam' and the SAB parenthetical note is correct: Jude is quoting 1 Enoch 60:8, not Genesis. The contradiction is really about where your counting starts.
entries.commentary: This one should probably get flagged for human review because it hinges on whether inclusive counting is considered a contradiction at all. The ancient convention, and the one Jude uses, is inclusive counting: Adam is position one, Enoch is position seven. Genesis 5:3-18 lists Adam → Seth → Enos → Cainan → Mahalaleel → Jared → Enoch, which is seven names inclusive and six generations. Luke 3:37-38 and 1 Chronicles 1:1-2 just list the names; they don't specify a count, so the SAB's 'sixth from Adam' framing is an inference by the author, not a claim made by Luke or Chronicles themselves. Richard Bauckham's Jude, 2 Peter commentary in the Word Biblical Commentary and James VanderKam's extensive work on the Enochic literature both note that 'seventh from Adam' is a stock epithet in Second Temple Jewish sources (1 Enoch 60:8, 93:3; Jubilees 7:39) and carries significance — the seventh generation is a position of sabbatical completion and cosmic authority in apocalyptic literature. So Jude is invoking an established Enochic tradition, not miscounting Genesis. The contradiction as stated is weak — it's really a dispute about counting convention. Recommend the SAB rewrite this one around Jude's use of 1 Enoch as scripture, which is a much stronger contradiction (canonical issues).

entries.question: Must everyone die?
entries.summary: Romans 5:12 says death passed upon all men through Adam. Hebrews 9:27 says it is appointed unto men once to die. Genesis 5:24 and Hebrews 11:5 then say Enoch was taken by God and did not see death — and 2 Kings 2:11 does the same for Elijah. The universal claim has named exceptions.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist move is to read 'all' and 'appointed' as referring to the general rule, not an absolute law. Archer, Blomberg, and the ESV Study Bible notes all treat Enoch and Elijah as special divine exceptions that don't invalidate the general principle. That framing is internally consistent if you're willing to grant that 'all' doesn't mean all. The critical read just notes the text itself is polyphonic. N.T. Wright's Resurrection of the Son of God and John Collins in his work on Daniel and apocalyptic traditions both trace how Second Temple Judaism developed the 'ascension' or 'translation' motif for righteous figures — Enoch in 1 Enoch and 2 Enoch, Elijah in 2 Kings and later Jewish sources, Moses in some traditions. Hebrews 11:5 explicitly affirms Enoch 'did not see death.' So you've got one biblical stream affirming universal death as the consequence of the fall, and another stream preserving elite exceptions. Paul's Romans 5 argument requires universality for its theological work, but the author of Hebrews happily holds both ideas simultaneously. The contradiction is real but the harmonization — 'general rule with exceptions' — is at least coherent. Call it a soft contradiction that the text itself acknowledges without resolving.

entries.question: Who was Noah's youngest son?
entries.summary: Genesis 9:24 calls Ham Noah's 'younger son' after the nakedness episode. Genesis 5:32, 6:10, 7:13, 9:18, 10:1, and 1 Chronicles 1:4 consistently list the sons as Shem, Ham, and Japheth — an order that, read as birth order, makes Japheth the youngest. Either the listing order is wrong or the 'younger son' label is wrong.
entries.commentary: Apologists push back on the assumption that the Shem-Ham-Japheth listing order reflects birth order. Kenneth Mathews in the New American Commentary on Genesis and Hamilton's NICOT Genesis both argue the listing order is thematic or theological (Shem first because of the messianic line, Japheth last for narrative reasons), not chronological. Genesis 10:21 in the Masoretic Text is itself ambiguous — the Hebrew can be read as either 'Shem, the older brother of Japheth' or 'Shem, the brother of Japheth the elder,' and translations split on it. That ambiguity is real. But it doesn't solve the core problem: Genesis 9:24 calls Ham specifically the 'younger son' (ha-qaton, literally 'the small/little one'), not Japheth. Claus Westermann and Gordon Wenham both note this is a genuine inconsistency between sources. Friedman's Sources Revealed assigns the nakedness episode and the genealogical frame to different hands. The cleanest read is that the redactor stitched together a J-style Noah-vineyard narrative (where Ham is the youngest son whose sin justifies the curse on Canaan) with a P-style genealogy (where the three sons appear in a fixed Shem-Ham-Japheth order for theological reasons). The seam shows. The harmonization requires declaring the listing order non-chronological, which works — but only by conceding that the text isn't giving consistent birth-order information.

entries.question: How many sons are there?
entries.summary: John 3:18 and 1 John 4:9 call Jesus the 'only begotten Son of God' (monogenes). Luke 3:38 calls Adam the son of God. Romans 8:14 and a dozen other Pauline passages call everyone led by the Spirit a son of God. The Bible uses 'son of God' for Jesus exclusively, for humanity collectively, and for individual believers — three overlapping uses that don't cleanly map onto each other.
entries.commentary: This is a three-way structural contradiction that the apologist harmonization actually handles reasonably well — up to a point. The standard move, running from Augustine through D. A. Carson's Pillar commentary on John, is to distinguish senses: Jesus is the Son of God ontologically (unique, eternal), humans are sons of God by creation (Adam) or adoption (believers). The Greek word monogenes is the key term — Carson and Köstenberger defend the translation 'one of a kind' or 'unique,' not literally 'only begotten.' That linguistic move is defensible; recent scholarship by Charles Lee Irons and others has done real work on monogenes. But here's the critical wrinkle. Divine sonship language in the Hebrew Bible is promiscuous — angels are 'sons of God' (Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7; Gen 6:2), Israel collectively is God's son (Exod 4:22, Hos 11:1), the Davidic king is God's son (Ps 2:7, 2 Sam 7:14). Michael Peppard's The Son of God in the Roman World and Adela Yarbro Collins and John Collins in King and Messiah as Son of God trace how first-century divine-sonship language was far broader than later Nicene Trinitarian categories admit. John's 'only begotten' is a theological power move staking an exclusive claim that the rest of the canon doesn't support. The Bible uses 'son of God' in at least four distinct senses. The contradiction isn't that they can't all be reconciled — it's that the reconciliation requires importing Nicene categories the underlying texts don't have.

entries.question: Do angels have sex?
entries.summary: Genesis 6:2-4 and Jude 6-7 describe angelic beings (the 'sons of God') having sex with human women and producing Nephilim. Genesis 19 has the Sodomites attempting to rape two angelic visitors. Mark 12:25 then has Jesus saying angels in heaven neither marry nor are given in marriage. The Bible's angelic sexuality is inconsistent — actively horny in Genesis and Jude, genderless in the Synoptics.
entries.commentary: Apologists try to split this two ways. First, they reinterpret Genesis 6:2 so the 'sons of God' are not angels at all but the godly Sethite line, with 'daughters of men' as wicked Cainite women. Archer and Hamilton both run this move. Second, they note Jesus says angels don't marry 'in heaven' — which leaves open the possibility of fallen angels acting otherwise. The Sethite reading is a post-biblical rationalization. Michael Heiser in The Unseen Realm, Loren Stuckenbruck's work on 1 Enoch, and James VanderKam all document that Second Temple Judaism unanimously read Genesis 6:2 as referring to angelic beings — it's the standard reading in 1 Enoch 6-11, Jubilees 5, the Damascus Document, Josephus, Philo, and the New Testament authors including Jude and 2 Peter. Jude 6-7 explicitly glosses Genesis 6 as angels 'going after strange flesh' (sarkos heteras). The Sethite interpretation only emerges in the third and fourth centuries CE with Julius Africanus and Augustine, largely motivated by theological embarrassment at the earlier reading. So the contradiction is real: early biblical writers held that a category of divine beings sexually interacted with humans, and the Synoptic Jesus treats angels as categorically asexual. The harmonization requires throwing out the Second Temple consensus reading of Genesis 6.

entries.question: Was God satisfied with his creation?
entries.summary: Genesis 1:31 has God pronouncing everything he made 'very good' on day six. Five chapters later, in Genesis 6:6-7, God repents that he ever made humanity and resolves to destroy it all. The satisfaction of Genesis 1 becomes divine regret by Genesis 6.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization here is clean on paper: Genesis 1's 'very good' was the pre-fall state, and Genesis 6's grief reflects the corruption that followed the fall and the Nephilim episode — humans ruined the good creation; God didn't revise his own assessment. Walton, Kidner, and Mathews all run this. That reading works grammatically and preserves divine immutability. The critical read comes from source criticism. Richard Friedman, Joel Baden, and David Carr all identify Genesis 1:31 as Priestly (P) and Genesis 6:5-8 as Yahwistic (J). They are different authors with different theologies of God. P's creation is cosmically ordered and good by divine fiat; J's God is more volatile, learns from experience, and emotionally reacts to events. James Kugel in How to Read the Bible calls this the 'small God' of J versus the cosmic God of P. The 'repented' of Genesis 6:6 (Hebrew nicham) is the same word used in 1 Samuel 15:11 and 15:35 where Yahweh regrets making Saul king — a genuinely mutable deity. The harmonization works only if you flatten two distinct authorial voices into one. The critical read respects what each source actually says: P's God surveys his work with satisfaction; J's God feels genuine disappointment, to the point of deciding to start over. Different theologies, same canon.

entries.question: God does repent?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Numbers, 1 Samuel, Psalms, Ezekiel, Joel, Jonah, Malachi, James
entries.summary: Numbers 23:19, 1 Samuel 15:29, Malachi 3:6, and James 1:17 stack hard on the idea that God does not and cannot repent or change. Genesis 6:6, Joel 2:14, and Jonah 3:10 show God actively repenting — changing his mind about punishment, grieving the creation of humanity. The Bible contradicts itself on whether Yahweh is mutable.
entries.commentary: Classical theologians from Augustine through Aquinas resolved this by declaring divine impassibility a metaphysical doctrine and the 'repent' verses as anthropopathic accommodation — God speaks in human emotional categories but doesn't actually experience them. That is the apologist playbook on this contradiction, and you'll find versions of it in Archer's Encyclopedia and in the Westminster theological tradition. The problem is the text itself doesn't read that way. 1 Samuel 15 is especially devastating for the harmonization: verse 11 has Yahweh saying 'It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king,' verse 29 has Samuel insisting 'the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent,' and verse 35 closes the chapter with 'the LORD repented that he had made Saul king.' The same chapter asserts both positions. Terence Fretheim in The Suffering of God and Walter Brueggemann in his Theology of the Old Testament both argue that divine mutability is a genuine feature of Hebrew Bible theology, not an embarrassment to be explained away. Open theists like Gregory Boyd take this further, arguing the 'doesn't repent' verses are the outliers inserted to defend a later philosophical doctrine of immutability. Whichever way you slice it — source-critical, open theist, classical — the text is saying both things. The harmonization works only by privileging the metaphysical verses over the narrative ones, which is a theological choice, not an exegetical result.

entries.question: Has there ever been a just person?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos, Habakkuk, Tobit, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts, Romans, Galatians, Titus, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter
entries.summary: Ecclesiastes 7:20 flatly denies there is any just man on earth who does good and does not sin. Paul echoes this in Romans 3:10. But the biblical corpus is stuffed with named figures — Noah, Lot, Joseph, Simeon, John the Baptist, Joseph of Arimathea, Cornelius — explicitly called just, and Proverbs and the Deuterocanon run hundreds of verses on what just people are and do. The no-one-is-just claim and the roster of just people cannot both be literally true.
entries.commentary: The apologist move here, running from Augustine through Calvin through modern Reformed commentators, is the imputed-versus-inherent righteousness distinction. No one is intrinsically just (Ecclesiastes, Romans 3), but specific individuals are called just because God reckons them so, or because they meet a covenantal standard even while sinning. Doug Moo's NICNT Romans commentary runs a version of this. That is a defensible theological harmonization — but it imports the Pauline-Augustinian soteriological framework onto a Hebrew Bible that doesn't obviously share it. The critical read is that 'just' (tsaddiq in Hebrew, dikaios in Greek) operates at different levels across different sources. In the Priestly and Deuteronomistic materials, righteousness is covenant fidelity — observable behavior that a community can assess. In Ecclesiastes, a late skeptical sapiential work, the author is making a rhetorical universalist claim about human limitation that isn't interested in the covenantal usage. Romans 3:10 is Paul pasting together a catena of psalm and wisdom verses for rhetorical effect; Richard Hays in Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul shows how loose Paul's use of the Old Testament catena actually is. So the texts are talking past each other. The contradiction is flattened only by privileging Paul's Augustinian reading as the hermeneutical key. The plain sense is that the Hebrew Bible is happy to call specific people just, and the later universalist sin-language is a theological innovation.

entries.question: Does God approve of slavery?
entries.summary: Genesis 9:25-27 has Noah — explicitly called a just and righteous man — pronouncing a divine curse condemning Canaan to be 'a servant of servants,' and the Torah then provides extensive regulations for Hebrew and foreign slavery without ever abolishing it. Against that, the 'love thy neighbor' command of Leviticus 19:18, quoted by Jesus in Mark 12:31 and Matthew 22:39, makes slavery ethically untenable. The Torah builds the institution; the prophetic and Jesus ethic undercuts it.
entries.commentary: Apologists handle this through progressive revelation and accommodation. Paul Copan's Is God a Moral Monster? and John Walton's ancient-Near-Eastern framing both argue that biblical slavery was a different institution from chattel slavery — more like indentured servitude, with protections unavailable in surrounding cultures. The Jubilee laws, Sabbath release, and the prohibition on returning runaway slaves (Deut 23:15-16) get foregrounded. That steel-man has real textual support for Hebrew slaves specifically. But it collapses when you look at the treatment of foreign slaves. Leviticus 25:44-46 explicitly permits Israelites to buy chattel slaves from surrounding nations as permanent inheritable property. Exodus 21:20-21 permits beating a slave to death if the slave lingers a day or two before dying, because 'he is his money.' Hector Avalos's Slavery, Abolitionism, and the Ethics of Biblical Scholarship and Jennifer Glancy's Slavery in Early Christianity both document that the Bible's slavery laws were used by pro-slavery theologians in the antebellum South precisely because they're actually there — not as misreadings but as accurate citation. Jesus' 'love thy neighbor' commandment never once explicitly bans slavery, and Paul's Philemon sends a runaway back. The contradiction is real: the Bible regulates slavery extensively, never forbids it, and holds a neighbor-love ethic that logically should forbid it. The harmonization works only by picking which verses get to define 'God's position.'

entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, 2 Samuel, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Malachi, Matthew, Luke, Romans, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, Revelation
entries.summary: Job 15:14, Isaiah 64:6, and Romans 3:10 deny anyone is righteous — all our righteousness is as filthy rags, there is none righteous, no, not one. Hebrews 11:4, 2 Peter 2:5-8, Ezekiel 14:14, Luke 1:6, and Matthew 23:35 name specific righteous people — Abel, Noah, Lot, Daniel, Job, Elisabeth, Zacharias. Same contradiction structure as id=35 but with 'righteous' instead of 'just.'
entries.commentary: This entry has a scrape artifact — answer id=81 contains both the 'No' and 'Yes' content concatenated, and answer id=82 duplicates the 'Yes' content. The underlying contradiction is structurally identical to id=35 and resolves the same way. The apologist harmonization is imputed versus inherent righteousness: no one is intrinsically righteous, but God reckons certain individuals righteous by faith. This is Paul's argument in Romans 4 and it has been the dominant Protestant read since the Reformation. Doug Moo's Romans commentary and N. T. Wright's Justification both run this. The critical read is the same as id=35 — different biblical authors use 'righteous' (tsaddiq, dikaios) at different levels of abstraction. Ezekiel 14:14 names Noah, Daniel, and Job as paradigmatic righteous individuals in a way that assumes righteousness is a real and identifiable quality. Job 15:14 is from Eliphaz, one of the friends whose theology Yahweh ultimately rebukes in Job 42:7-8 — so quoting it as a flat theological statement is already a methodological mistake. Isaiah 64:6 is a communal lament, rhetorical language about exile, not a dogmatic anthropological claim. Paul then takes these context-bound statements and redeploys them in Romans 3 as a universal proof-text catena. Richard Hays and Francis Watson both analyze this Pauline hermeneutic at length. The Bible names people righteous in one voice and denies anyone is righteous in another voice, and the second voice is partly constructed by pulling verses out of their argumentative contexts. entries.question: To kill or not to kill
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, Ecclesiastes, Matthew, Mark, Luke
entries.summary: Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17 command 'thou shalt not kill,' and Jesus reaffirms it in Mark 10:19 and Luke 18:20. The same Torah then mandates capital punishment for witches, adulterers, gay men, non-virgin brides, blasphemers, sabbath breakers, and disobedient children. Yahweh himself repeatedly orders genocide — most infamously 1 Samuel 15:3's command to slaughter Amalekite infants and suckling children. The sixth commandment sits inside a legal code that demands killing on almost every other page.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist move is lexical: the Hebrew verb ratsach in Exodus 20:13 means 'murder' — unlawful killing — not all killing. Judicial execution and commanded warfare fall outside the prohibition. Archer, Copan, and the NASB translation all run this. The lexical claim is partly correct — ratsach is narrower than the broader harag or hemit — but not as clean as apologists want. Wilma Ann Bailey's You Shall Not Kill or You Shall Not Murder? shows that ratsach appears in contexts including accidental manslaughter (Num 35:22-25), where 'murder' is the wrong translation. So the sixth commandment's scope is ambiguous even before you get to the contradiction with the commanded killings. But the harder problem isn't translation — it's that Yahweh is giving the 'thou shalt not' and also issuing the execution orders and herem warfare commands in the same corpus. The harmonization has to argue that divine commands override the general prohibition, which functionally means: don't kill unless God tells you to, in which case kill everything including babies. Philip Jenkins's Laying Down the Sword and Eric Seibert's The Violence of Scripture both engage this directly. The critical verdict is that the Pentateuch preserves competing theologies of killing — a humanitarian decalogue stream and a herem/genocidal stream — and the New Testament Jesus generally sides with the decalogue stream while quietly ignoring the other. The apologetic lexical fix lets Exodus 20:13 survive the commanded killings but it doesn't resolve the moral tension; it just relocates it.

entries.question: When did Noah enter the ark?
entries.summary: Genesis 7:7-10 has Noah and family entering the ark, and then seven days later the flood waters come. Genesis 7:11-13 places Noah and family entering the ark on the 'selfsame day' the fountains of the deep broke open and the rain began. Same flood, two entry timings, four verses apart.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization is that 7:7-10 describes the initial entry with livestock still being loaded, and 7:11-13 describes the final closing-up on the day the rains began. Archer runs this move, and you'll find versions of it in evangelical study Bibles. That reading is possible in isolation but it requires reading 'in the selfsame day entered Noah' as 'on the selfsame day Noah was already inside and the door was shut,' which is not what the Hebrew says. The critical read is cleaner and has been the scholarly consensus since Wellhausen. Genesis 7 is a classic double-narrative from the Documentary Hypothesis, interweaving J (Yahwist) and P (Priestly) flood accounts. Friedman's Sources Revealed separates them: the J strand gives the seven-day prediction and the animals-by-seven-pairs count; the P strand gives the exact dating ('the 600th year... the second month... the seventeenth day') and the animals-by-twos count. Gordon Wenham's WBC Genesis volume, even from a more conservative angle, concedes the source seam. Joel Baden's Composition of the Pentateuch walks through the flood narrative as the textbook case for the Documentary Hypothesis precisely because the doublets are so clean. Two sources, two timings of entry, one redactor who put them side by side without smoothing them. The contradiction is a source-critical fingerprint.
